It is called a keel-worm only by people who have never touched one. On its world there is no sun, no star-glint, no moon—only stone, brine, and the slow heat of a buried core. The animal lives in that permanent dark the way a fish lives in water: the absence is not a lack it notices.

Its body is a long, low ribbon, about the length of a human arm and no thicker than a wrist, flattened so it can slide through silt without lifting a wake that predators could hear. The skin is not pale in any way that matters; pigment is useless here. It is smooth, slightly translucent, and always faintly warmer than the mud around it, because the creature spends much of its life pressed to thin places in the crust where heat seeps up. That warmth is both comfort and camouflage. Things that hunt by temperature learn to ignore a shape that matches the vent.

It has no eyes. Where a head might be expected there is only a blunt, shovel-shaped prow armored with a plate of mineral the animal secretes from metals dissolved in the water. Along the rim of that plate sit pits—dozens of them—each lined with cells that taste the chemistry of the current: sulfur, metal ions, the faint sourness of another animal’s breath. Behind the plate, two long feelers trail like unspooled thread. They are not for grasping. They read pressure. A footfall on the seafloor a body-length away bends the water just enough for those threads to stiffen, and the keel-worm freezes, flush with the mud, until the disturbance passes.

Down the midline of its back runs a low ridge of stiff bristles. They are not weapons. They are ears. Every bristle is tuned to a different shiver in the ground—the crack of cooling rock, the rasp of a burrower, the low drum of something large turning over in the dark. The animal “sees” by the pattern those bristles make against its nerves: a map of motion, redrawn every few heartbeats.

It feeds without biting in any familiar sense. The underside of the prow is a soft, folded mouth that everts like a glove turned inside out, presses to bacterial mats, and scrapes them up with microscopic combs. When prey is near—small, blind crustacean-things that click as they walk—the keel-worm does not lunge. It waits until the clicks are directly overhead, then humps its body and slaps the silt, stunning the prey with a pressure wave. The mouth finds it by taste alone.

Reproduction is a matter of chemistry, not display. When two keel-worms meet, each releases a thin slick of signal-molecules into the boundary layer of water hugging the mud. If the signatures match, they lie parallel, prow to tail, and exchange packets of tissue through pores along their flanks. There is no courtship visible to any eye, because there are no eyes to see it. Afterward they part without touching again. Young emerge already shovel-headed, already listening, already unable to imagine light.

What it knows of its world is a continuum of gradients: warmer, colder, metal-rich, metal-poor, still, disturbed. Distance is how long a tremor takes to arrive. Danger is a taste that arrives before a sound. Home is the patch of crust whose heat and chemistry match the pattern it memorized as a hatchling. In that sense the keel-worm is not blind. It is simply built for a planet that never bothered to invent sight.

A vell is about the size of a wolf and shaped more like a flattened, jointless question mark. Its skin is pale, almost translucent, and permanently damp—a thin film of mucus that conducts chemical signals and keeps sensory organs from drying in the thin, cold air. There are no eyes, not even vestigial pits. The skull is a smooth dome of cartilage. It does not walk so much as flow. Six short, muscular pads grip the rock; between them, the belly can inflate and deflate, letting the animal hover a finger’s width above the ground on a cushion of exhaled air when the surface is treacherous. Plants, in any ordinary sense, do not exist. The base of the food web is microbial mats fed by chemical energy: hydrogen, methane, reduced iron, sulfur. Danger is a sudden stillness in the pressure field, followed by a smell that does not belong to anything that grazes mats.

Color is meaningless to it, but if you could shine a lamp it would look like wet basalt: matte, slightly iridescent only where mineral salts have crusted in the pores. Those pores are not decoration. They drink dissolved metals and vent gases. It navigates by taste-maps older than any memory. A rich vent smells like a road. A dead vent smells like a closed door.

It has no jaws. The narrow end of the body is a muscular siphon. When it finds a mat of chemosynthetic microbes—pale, heat-loving films that grow where hot water leaks through rock—it presses the siphon down and pulses, drawing the film and the silt beneath it into a gut that is more filter than stomach. The microbes are not plants. They burn hydrogen sulfide and methane the way leaves burn light. The silt-singer burns the microbes. Everything edible on this world is either a chemical engine or something that ate one.

Locomotion is a slow accordion crawl. Rings of muscle contract in waves, gripping with thousands of microscopic hooks made of the same mineral the creature precipitates from the water—calcium, silica, a little iron.
